topic: Undo/revert/rewind separation and safe recovery UX
research_questions: How do mature version-control, IDE, chat, and agent products distinguish undo, revert, rewind, checkpoint restore, and destructive recovery?
Which user-visible confirmations, previews, scopes, and recovery guarantees prevent accidental loss or ambiguous rollback?
How should Puppet Master represent operation identity, affected artifacts, provenance, reversibility, and partial failure across these recovery modes?
Which failure modes and accessibility or trust signals are documented by official or primary sources?

sources.title: Git - git-reset Documentation
sources.material_relevance: Defines reset as changing the commit pointed to by HEAD or updating the index, with mode-specific effects on the working tree; documents ORIG_HEAD, path limits, hard overwrite behavior, merge/keep abort conditions, and the distinction from restore and revert.

sources.title: Git - git-revert Documentation
sources.material_relevance: Defines revert as recording new commits that reverse earlier commits, requires a clean working tree for the normal operation, and documents continue, skip, quit, and abort states for interrupted or conflicted sequences.

sources.title: Git - git-restore Documentation
sources.material_relevance: Defines content restoration for selected paths from a source, including separate index and working-tree scopes, and warns that tracked paths absent from the source are removed to match it.

sources.title: Git - git-reflog Documentation
sources.material_relevance: Documents local reference logs that record prior branch and reference tips and expose prior values such as HEAD@{2}, while also documenting expiration and deletion of recovery records.

sources.title: User interface - Timeline and local file history
sources.material_relevance: Describes a unified file timeline containing Git commits and local saves, full-content local history entries, diff/compare and restore actions, deleted-file recovery, and configurable size, count, exclusion, and merge-window limits.

sources.title: Revert changes with checkpoints and editing requests
sources.material_relevance: Separates editing a prior chat request from restoring a file checkpoint, snapshots affected files before each request, requires confirmation, shows optional file and line-change details, supports redo after restore, and supports forking while preserving the original conversation.

sources.title: Local History
sources.material_relevance: Shows IDE-local revisions independent of version control, diff-based restoration of fragments, files, deleted files, folders, or projects, labels for meaningful states, and explicit retention and lifecycle limits that make it a recovery aid rather than durable history.

sources.title: Checkpointing
sources.material_relevance: Separates restoring code, restoring conversation, restoring both, and summarizing context; records checkpoints around prompts, exposes a rewind menu, and explicitly limits coverage for Bash changes, external changes, concurrent sessions, retention, and permanent version history.

sources.title: Undo and redo
sources.material_relevance: Provides platform guidance to make undo and redo outcomes predictable, label the target operation, highlight the changed content, support multiple logical undos, and avoid confusing gesture redefinitions.

sources.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
sources.material_relevance: Defines reversible, checked, or confirmed error-prevention options for data modification and deletion, plus programmatically determinable names, roles, states, and status messages for assistive technologies.

sources.title: Commands - JupyterLab 4.6.1 documentation
sources.material_relevance: Uses an explicit user-facing command label, Revert to Checkpoint, demonstrating that checkpoint restoration is named as a distinct operation rather than silently conflated with ordinary editor undo.

sources.title: Crab: A Semantics-Aware Checkpoint/Restore Runtime for Agent Sandboxes
sources.material_relevance: Primary research frames agent recovery as a state-spanning problem across filesystems, processes, and runtime artifacts, identifies the agent-OS semantic gap, and evaluates checkpoint granularity and recovery correctness beyond chat history alone.

findings.claim: Mature version control treats revert, reset, and restore as different state transitions: revert records a new commit that reverses an earlier commit; reset moves a reference and may also change the index or working tree; restore projects selected paths from a source into the index and/or working tree.
findings.notes: The operation name encodes both the target layer and whether history is appended, moved, or merely projected into files.

findings.claim: Destructive recovery is not equivalent to reversible correction: Git documents reset --hard as overwriting the working tree and potentially untracked files, while reflog and ORIG_HEAD are separate local recovery handles rather than a promise that a user-facing operation is automatically reversible forever.
findings.notes: The existence and expiration of a reflog does not turn a destructive command into an indefinitely durable undo.

findings.claim: IDE recovery surfaces expose history at artifact scope: VS Code combines Git commits and local saves in a timeline with diffs and restore actions, and JetBrains Local History supports restoring a selected fragment, file, deleted file, folder, or project state.
findings.notes: The user can choose a narrower artifact scope than the last global action, which is materially different from repeatedly pressing undo.

findings.claim: Agent products split recovery along independent conversation and artifact axes: VS Code distinguishes editing a prior request from restoring a checkpoint and provides redo and fork; Claude Code separately offers restore code, restore conversation, restore both, and summarize without changing files.
findings.notes: A generic rewind label is insufficient when the user may want to change context, code, both, or neither.

findings.claim: Agent checkpoints are bounded coverage mechanisms, not complete transaction logs: Claude Code does not track Bash-created file changes, ordinary external edits, or most concurrent-session changes, and its checkpoints are described as session-level complements to permanent version control.
findings.notes: The coverage boundary must be visible before a user interprets a successful restore as complete workspace recovery.

findings.claim: Undo safety depends on outcome predictability and visibility: Apple recommends descriptive operation labels, highlighting the result, and allowing repeated logical undos; WCAG frames data deletion or modification as requiring reversibility, checking, or review and confirmation, and requires status information to be available to assistive technologies.
findings.notes: Trust signals are functional recovery controls, not decorative copy: they prevent repeated or mis-scoped rollback.

findings.claim: Partial failure is a first-class recovery state in mature tooling: Git revert exposes continue, skip, quit, and abort after a sequence or conflict, while Git reset documents modes that abort when local changes would be overwritten.
findings.notes: A recovery action needs a resumable or abortable lifecycle rather than a binary success toast.

findings.claim: Checkpoint products make the target state inspectable before execution: VS Code can show files and line deltas per request and asks for confirmation before restoring; JupyterLab exposes a named Revert to Checkpoint action.
findings.notes: The explicit checkpoint target and change summary reduce the ambiguity of an unlabeled rollback control.

findings.claim: Agent recovery must account for process and runtime effects, not only chat and file contents: the primary Crab study identifies an agent-OS semantic gap in which application-level recovery can miss OS-side effects and evaluates checkpoint granularity across sandbox state.
findings.notes: The paper is primary research and its reported measurements should be treated as evidence for the problem shape, not as a universal Puppet Master performance guarantee.

findings.claim: Puppet Master should model recovery as a typed operation over a declared state vector rather than as a single undo stack; this is an inference from the distinct Git layers, IDE artifact scopes, agent code/conversation axes, and side-effect coverage boundaries.
findings.notes: The recommendation synthesizes the sources; no source uses Puppet Master's exact data model.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: History-preserving revert: reverse a known committed change by appending a new, attributable commit rather than erasing the original history.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Use a forward recovery record for shared or published plan changes, retaining the original operation, actor, target, and reason in provenance.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Reference rewind: move a branch or pointer to an earlier commit, with explicit modes deciding whether the index and working tree are preserved, merged, or overwritten.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Expose ref, index, working-tree, and path scope separately; never present a hard rewind as an ordinary content undo.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Path restoration: restore selected artifacts from a named source revision, optionally affecting staged state and working-tree state independently.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Permit selective artifact recovery and show when the target source lacks a path, because the resulting action may delete that path.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Layered local history: IDEs provide a diffable, artifact-scoped local revision stream that can restore fragments or deleted files, but retention, size, and product lifecycle limit its durability.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Label local checkpoints with coverage and retention guarantees and distinguish them from durable repository history.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Request-bound agent checkpoint: snapshot affected files around a chat or agent request, then restore a whole request batch, redo it, edit the request, or fork from the checkpoint.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Give each agent operation a visible checkpoint boundary and an explicit distinction between restoring state, re-running a request, and forking an alternative.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Two-axis agent rewind: restore code, conversation, both, or context summary as separate choices, with summary preserving files and restore changing state.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Use separate state scopes in the recovery confirmation so a user cannot accidentally discard useful conversation while trying to restore artifacts, or vice versa.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Named checkpoint restoration: notebook tooling names checkpoint recovery directly as Revert to Checkpoint rather than leaving the target implicit in a generic undo affordance.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Use stable checkpoint labels, timestamps, and operation descriptions instead of relying only on ordinal undo depth.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Local reference recovery: a reflog records prior reference tips and can identify where a ref used to point, but entries can be expired or deleted.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Treat recovery handles as expiring evidence with explicit retention metadata, not as an invisible infinite undo contract.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Outcome-forward undo UX: describe the operation, show where the result landed, support repeated logical undo, and avoid ambiguous controls or redefined standard gestures.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Make recovery feedback identify the operation and affected artifacts in text and visual focus, with keyboard-accessible controls.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Semantic checkpoint coverage: research on agent sandboxes distinguishes chat-visible actions from filesystem, process, and runtime effects and argues for checkpoint granularity that follows recovery-relevant effects.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Record side-effect coverage and observation limits alongside every checkpoint so a successful file restore is not mistaken for a complete runtime rollback.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A user chooses a broad reset or rewind when they intended a single-file or single-hunk correction, overwriting unrelated work.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Preflight the exact state layers and artifact set; show a diff and counts for all affected artifacts; default to selective restore where the requested scope is ambiguous; require an escalated confirmation for working-tree overwrite.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A history rewrite is applied to a shared or already published branch, creating divergence or making collaborators lose the expected reference.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Show target ref visibility and publication state; prefer a new compensating revert record for shared history; require an explicit destructive-rewrite acknowledgement for pointer movement.

failure_modes.failure_mode: Uncommitted or concurrent changes collide with a restore, so some files cannot be safely changed or the operation silently discards local work.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Run a freshness and conflict preflight, show dirty and concurrent artifacts, preserve a pre-operation snapshot, and expose abort or continue states rather than presenting a partial result as success.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A path restore targets a source in which the path is absent, causing deletion, or the user misunderstands whether staged state, working-tree state, or both will change.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Separate index and working-tree scope controls, list paths that will be removed, and show the source revision and resulting state in the confirmation preview.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A local-history or checkpoint entry is missing because it exceeded size or count limits, expired, was cleared by product lifecycle, or was never captured.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Display capture status, retention horizon, and durability tier on each recovery point; offer a durable commit or export path before high-risk work; never promise recovery where coverage is absent.

failure_modes.failure_mode: An agent checkpoint restores tracked file edits but leaves Bash-created files, external systems, process state, or concurrent-session changes in place, producing a semantically inconsistent workspace.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Attach a side-effect inventory and coverage class to the checkpoint; distinguish file-only recovery from process/runtime recovery; surface commands and external effects that are outside the restore envelope and require compensating actions.

failure_modes.failure_mode: The user wants to restore code but the control also rewinds conversation, or wants to change the prompt but the control removes later state, creating code/context divergence.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Make code state, conversation state, and prompt replay separate selectable scopes; show the post-operation state for each scope and provide redo or fork when available.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A recovery partially succeeds or conflicts and the UI reports only a generic failure, leaving the user unsure which artifacts changed and whether retrying is safe.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Return per-artifact outcomes with before and after fingerprints, conflict or refusal reasons, an operation status of completed/partial/aborted, and an explicit next action; expose the status through programmatic notifications as well as visual UI.

failure_modes.failure_mode: The undo technically changes state outside the current viewport or focus, so the user assumes it did nothing and repeats the action, overshooting the intended recovery point.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Move focus or provide an explicit changed-artifact summary, announce the result, and use operation-specific labels rather than a bare Undo label.

implications.implication: Define a typed recovery operation with mode, target layer, source state, requested scope, and destructive-risk class; do not represent every recovery path as a single undo-stack entry.
implications.rationale: The source products use different semantics for history append, pointer movement, path projection, file checkpointing, conversation rewind, and summarization; a typed model prevents accidental semantic substitution.

implications.implication: Every recovery preview should enumerate affected artifacts, state layers, before and target revisions, expected removals, line or object deltas where available, and uncovered side effects.
implications.rationale: VS Code exposes diffs and file/line changes, Git defines path and source semantics, and agent research shows file-only views can miss runtime effects.

implications.implication: Use provenance as a chain of compensating operations: preserve the original operation, the recovery operation, the selected source/checkpoint, actor and reason, and any superseding or fork relationship.
implications.rationale: Git's new revert commit and reflog preserve navigable history, while VS Code's fork and redo patterns avoid making recovery an unexplained destructive disappearance.

implications.implication: Represent reversibility as a scoped guarantee with coverage, retention, and expiry metadata, not as a boolean promise.
implications.rationale: IDE histories, agent checkpoints, and reflogs all document bounded persistence or coverage; the user must know what can still be recovered and from which layer.

implications.implication: Make partial failure an explicit terminal or resumable state with per-artifact results, conflict details, abort/continue controls, and a fresh safe retry point.
implications.rationale: Git exposes sequence lifecycle commands and refuses unsafe overwrites in some modes; WCAG requires users to be able to identify and correct errors rather than infer state from a generic message.

implications.implication: Separate artifact state from conversation state in both the data model and UI, and make replay, restore, summarize, and fork distinct operations.
implications.rationale: Both agent products document independent choices for file restoration, prompt editing, conversation restoration, summarization, redo, or fork; conflating them would remove a demonstrated safety distinction.

implications.implication: Treat accessibility and trust signals as part of recovery correctness: operation names, scope, changed-artifact feedback, keyboard path, focus management, and programmatic status must be available without relying on color or an invisible timeline.
implications.rationale: Apple links predictability and visible result feedback to avoiding repeated undo, while WCAG requires review/reversibility and machine-readable status for assistive technology.

implications.implication: For agent-driven operations, store a side-effect inventory or observation boundary alongside file diffs so runtime recovery does not claim more than it can restore.
implications.rationale: Claude documents untracked command and external changes, and the primary study describes the same semantic gap across filesystem, process, and runtime state.

novel_ideas.idea: Recovery envelope: persist one envelope per operation containing operation_id, mode, target state layer, selected artifact set, before and target fingerprints, provenance links, capture timestamp, retention deadline, side-effect coverage, and compensating-operation slot.
novel_ideas.rationale: This combines Git's prior-reference evidence, IDE artifact history, agent checkpoint boundaries, and the research distinction between application and OS-visible effects into a single auditable recovery record.

novel_ideas.idea: Two-axis rewind sheet: present code/artifact state and conversation/context state as independent rows with separate checkboxes, previews, guarantees, and post-action links for restore, replay, summarize, or fork.
novel_ideas.rationale: The products already separate these actions; presenting them as explicit axes would make the distinction legible and reduce accidental code/context coupling.

novel_ideas.idea: Recovery safety ladder: ordinary undo for recent reversible edits, selective restore for artifact scope, checkpoint restore for bounded session batches, history-preserving revert for shared work, and destructive rewind only for explicitly private or disposable state.
novel_ideas.rationale: The ladder maps increasing blast radius and decreasing durability to increasingly explicit review, confirmation, and provenance requirements.

novel_ideas.idea: Coverage badge plus side-effect ledger: show a recovery point as file-complete, file-and-process-observed, or file-only/unknown, with a list of commands, external resources, concurrent writers, and runtime artifacts outside the envelope.
novel_ideas.rationale: This turns the documented agent checkpoint limitation and agent-OS semantic gap into a user-visible trust signal instead of a hidden caveat.

novel_ideas.idea: Transaction-style recovery preview: before execution, calculate a target diff, expected deletions, collision set, operation durability, and rollback-of-the-rollback handle; after execution, attach per-artifact fingerprints and a link to the compensating action.
novel_ideas.rationale: It operationalizes Git's preconditions and scope semantics, VS Code's file-change preview and redo, and WCAG's review-before-finalization principle.

novel_ideas.idea: Recovery receipt language: after every operation, state the exact mode, source checkpoint or revision, artifacts changed, artifacts skipped, uncovered effects, remaining recovery window, and next safe action in both a visible summary and an accessible status message.
novel_ideas.rationale: The pattern makes a successful, partial, aborted, or unavailable recovery observable and actionable instead of relying on a generic toast or an implicit timeline change.

unresolved_questions.question: Which Puppet Master state layers are authoritative for recovery: PlanUnit text, generated indexes, governance artifacts, user edits, runtime state, or external provider state, and which combinations may be restored atomically?

What is the minimum durable checkpoint guarantee that Puppet Master should make for a recovery point, and how should expiry or storage failure be surfaced before a destructive operation is authorized?

Can Puppet Master observe and compensate for non-file effects such as provider calls, spawned processes, generated outputs, or concurrent writers, or must every such effect be marked outside the recovery envelope?
Which recovery modes are allowed on shared or sealed plan state, and what authorization or review gate distinguishes a compensating revert from destructive pointer movement?

How should partial recovery be represented when an artifact graph crosses generated and source-owned nodes, and which artifacts must be blocked from independent restore to avoid a semantically invalid mixed state?
What user-facing vocabulary will Puppet Master standardize for undo, restore, rewind, revert, checkpoint, fork, replay, summarize, abort, and compensate across GUI and non-GUI surfaces?
Which accessibility APIs and Slint/web notification mechanisms will expose recovery scope, result, conflict, and expiry status without focus theft, color-only coding, or dependence on a visual diff?

What concurrency protocol prevents a stale checkpoint from being restored over newer edits, and should recovery fail closed, create a branch, or generate a conflict set when fingerprints no longer match?
